name: Surveyor 3
intro: Surveyor 3 was a robot lander sent to test the Moon’s ground before astronauts arrived. It bounced three times, settled on a slope inside a small crater, and dug the first trenches in lunar soil. Two and a half years later, two astronauts walked over and took parts of it home.
whyLeft: It was a one-way robot with no way to leave, and it never woke up after its first freezing two-week lunar night.
repurpose: It is a time capsule: comparing its metal, glass and paint with the parts Apollo 12 brought home would show what 57 more years on the Moon did.
funFact: Surveyor 3’s TV camera came home with Apollo 12 and is now on display at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

hotspots.title: Missing TV camera
hotspots.text: Scout, look closely: the TV camera that used to sit here is gone. On 20 November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean cut it off and carried it home so engineers could study how 31 months on the Moon had changed it.

photo.alt: A scientist looks through a microscope at Surveyor 3’s TV camera inside a clean cabinet
photo.caption: Back on Earth: a scientist inspects the real Surveyor 3 TV camera after Apollo 12 brought it home.

hotspots.title: Robot scoop
hotspots.text: This claw-like scoop dug the first trenches ever made on the Moon, up to 18 cm deep. It showed the soil was firm enough to hold up a landing spacecraft and an astronaut’s boots. Apollo 12 took the scoop home too.

photo.alt: Close-up of a Surveyor 3 footpad and its surface sampler scoop, photographed on the Moon
photo.caption: A footpad and the scoop of Surveyor 3, photographed by the Apollo 12 astronauts in 1969.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library, Apollo 12 photo AS12-48-7110 (NASA, public domain under NASA media guidelines)

hotspots.title: Bounce marks
hotspots.text: When Surveyor 3 landed, its radar was dazzled by the bright ground and its engines kept firing. It touched down, bounced about 20 m, touched again, hopped 11 m more and finally settled. Engineers on Earth had to send a command to shut the engines off.

hotspots.title: Solar panel
hotspots.text: Surveyor 3 ran on sunlight and batteries. After working all through its first two-week lunar day, it went silent after sunset on 3 May 1967 and never woke up from the long, freezing night. The panel is still here, but the battery behind it is long dead.

hotspots.title: Visitors from Earth
hotspots.text: Apollo 12’s lander Intrepid touched down only about 180 m away. Conrad and Bean walked down into this crater, photographed Surveyor 3 from every side and checked it like detectives before taking about 10 kg of parts.

photo.alt: An astronaut in a spacesuit stands beside Surveyor 3, with the Apollo 12 lunar module in the distance
photo.caption: An Apollo 12 astronaut checks Surveyor 3 in November 1969, with the lander Intrepid on the horizon.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library, Apollo 12 photo AS12-48-7133 (NASA, public domain under NASA media guidelines)

hotspots.title: Seen from orbit
hotspots.text: NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter can still spot Surveyor 3 from about 50 km up, along with the astronauts’ footpaths leading to it. Anyone planning a new visit could use these pictures as a map.
